clue.text: Singer offering note in jazz music feature in same production

indicators.note: in tells us the note is placed inside the word for jazz music

parts.note: swing is a style of big-band jazz
E is a musical note

indicators.note: the second in places the facial feature inside the jumbled letters
a production of something remakes it, so the letters of same are rearranged

parts.note: the chin is a feature of the face

explanation.surface: A singer gives a jazz performance with a note woven into the same production.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' poses as a vocalist but is the sewing-machine brand. 'production' rearranges the letters as MAES before the second 'in' fills them.
explanation.definitionFit: Singer is a famous manufacturer whose best-known products are machines for stitching cloth.

clue.text: Noted study (ho hum): pedestrian activity

parts.note: a ho-hum feeling of weariness is expressed with a sigh
walkers spend their time treading the pavement

explanation.surface: A dull study session, greeted with a weary ho-hum, compared to plodding along on foot.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Noted' means written in musical notes, not famous.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing music at first sight is studying a score full of written notes without rehearsal.

clue.text: Singularly I've been clumsy, so cry

indicators.note: singularly asks for the singular form, so the plural-looking final S is dropped

parts.note: whoops is what someone says after a clumsy slip

explanation.surface: Someone admits to their own awkwardness and lets out a yelp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singularly' treats the S of WHOOPS as if it were a plural ending and removes it.
explanation.definitionFit: A whoop is a loud shout of excitement or joy, a kind of cry.

clue.text: One proposing to the Queen of Jordan (unlikely man it's accepted)

indicators.note: accepted means the queen's name takes the jumbled letters inside it

parts.note: Queen Noor is the American-born widow of King Hussein of Jordan

indicators.note: unlikely suggests the letters of man it fall into an improbable new order

parts.note: the letters of man and it, the 's being a link meaning has

explanation.surface: Someone proposes marriage to Jordan's queen, an unlikely man being accepted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unlikely' rearranges the letters to MINAT; the 's of it's is just 'has', a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A nominator is a person who puts forward a candidate, so one who proposes a name.

clue.text: Little one goes into two, which goes into 1,100 — basic sort of division

indicators.note: the second goes into puts the whole construction within the Roman numerals for eleven hundred

parts.note: M is 1,000 and C is 100 in Roman numerals

indicators.note: goes into places the small child inside the Roman two

parts.note: II is two in Roman numerals
a tot is a small child

explanation.surface: A sum about numbers dividing into each other, described as basic division.
explanation.walkthrough: 'goes into' looks like arithmetic division but signals insertion twice, the first giving ITOTI. 'which' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Mitosis is the ordinary splitting of a cell into two, so the adjective describes that fundamental cell division.

clue.text: Musical no longer in vogue?

parts.note: chic means fashionable
ago refers to a time that has passed

explanation.surface: Asks whether a musical show has gone out of fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in reverse of the clue's order: 'in vogue' is CHIC and 'no longer' is AGO, giving the Kander and Ebb musical.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicago is a well-known Broadway musical about jazz-age murderesses.

clue.text: People making fish fingers heading off to river

indicators.note: heading off removes the first letter of the brand

parts.note: Findus is a frozen-food company famous in Britain for fish fingers

explanation.surface: A fish-finger firm loses its leader and heads for a river.
explanation.walkthrough: FINDUS is a British frozen-food brand; dropping its first letter leaves the great river of Pakistan.
explanation.definitionFit: The Indus is a major river flowing through Pakistan to the Arabian Sea.

clue.text: A singer poorly with two new heads — it's catching

indicators.note: poorly suggests the letters are in bad shape and need rearranging

parts.note: the head letter of new taken twice gives two Ns

explanation.surface: A sick singer with two new heads on, which sounds contagious.
explanation.walkthrough: 'poorly' rearranges A SINGER together with two Ns to make the answer; 'catching' is not an illness but trapping.
explanation.definitionFit: Ensnaring something means trapping or catching it, as in a snare.

clue.text: Tidy the latter half of where one eats

indicators.note: the latter half of keeps only the second five of the ten letters

parts.note: meals are taken in the dining room

explanation.surface: Instructions to tidy up the back end of an eating area.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the latter half of' drops DININ, the first five letters of DININGROOM.
explanation.definitionFit: To groom is to make neat and tidy, as with hair or a horse's coat.

clue.text: See 27
See 27
Bow in Peking oddly during minor blast

indicators.note: during places the odd letters inside the short blast

parts.note: a toot is a short blast on a horn

indicators.note: oddly takes the first, third and fifth letters of Peking

explanation.surface: A bow worn in Beijing during a little horn blast.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bow' looks like a verb or a ship's front but is a ribbon bow; 'in' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: A topknot is a ribbon bow or tuft worn on the crown of the head.

clue.text: Refuse sat festering in a refuse container

indicators.note: in places the jumbled letters inside the bin

parts.note: a bin holds rubbish

indicators.note: festering rubbish rots and changes, so the letters of sat are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone declines while sitting in rubbish rotting in a bin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Refuse' is a verb first, then rubbish. 'festering' turns SAT into STA, and 'in' places it in BIN.
explanation.definitionFit: To abstain is to decline or refrain, as when refusing to vote.

clue.text: Yarn spun around about shows style

indicators.note: around means the turned word goes about the other letter
spun suggests the word is turned around, read backwards

parts.note: a yarn is a tale or story
C is short for circa, about

explanation.surface: Telling a story with flair, a yarn spun about something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spun' turns TALE into ELAT, and 'around' wraps it round C.
explanation.definitionFit: Eclat means brilliance or flair of performance, a showy style.

clue.text: Reluctant to admit Mick's crook: if he's easily admitted, call one!

definitions.text: if he's easily admitted, call one

indicators.note: to admit means the word for reluctant takes the other letters inside

parts.note: loth means unwilling or reluctant

indicators.note: crook as an adjective means bad or unsound, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: the letters of Mick's, including the S

explanation.surface: Mick, a crook, is reluctant to confess; a joke follows about getting admitted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'crook' looks like a thief but is the Australian adjective for bad, signalling the rearrangement. Someone locked out wants to be easily admitted, so calls this tradesperson.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesperson who opens locks is the one to phone when you cannot get into your house.

clue.text: Bird's exact heart?

parts.note: the crux, Latin for cross, is the heart of a matter
to exact payment is to bill for it

explanation.surface: Asks what lies precisely at a bird's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: The pieces come in the reverse order to the clue. The '?' flags the loose link: crux is Latin for cross and means the heart of a matter.
explanation.definitionFit: The crossbill is a finch whose bill tips cross over, used for prising seeds from cones.

clue.text: Good character and bad one about to ruin one

indicators.note: about means the devil's name goes around the other letters

parts.note: Satan is the evil one
to mar is to spoil or ruin
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A good person and a bad one about to ruin someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Good character' points to the parable figure; 'to' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: The parable of the Good Samaritan makes the name stand for a kind, helpful person.

clue.text: Might one be touching up the Queen on Christmas Day, perhaps?

indicators.note: in an across clue on means placed after, so the speaker comes after the month

parts.note: Christmas Day falls in December, abbreviated Dec
the Queen gives a speech on Christmas Day, so she is a speaker

explanation.surface: A risque question about someone groping the Queen at Christmas.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touching up' suggests groping, but means repainting. The Queen's Christmas broadcast makes her a December speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter and decorator touches up walls and woodwork with fresh paint.

clue.text: Tempestuous Rent-a-Party?

parts.note: rent is the past tense of rend, meaning torn
a do is a party

explanation.surface: A stormy party hired for the evening.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rent' looks like hire but is the past of rend, TORN; a stormy wind tearing up a party.
explanation.definitionFit: A violent rotating windstorm is the epitome of something tempestuous that tears things apart.

clue.text: Financial centre almost entering tangible performance

indicators.note: entering puts the shortened financial district inside the word for tangible

parts.note: something tangible is real

indicators.note: almost drops the final letter

parts.note: the City is London's financial district

explanation.surface: Money from the City goes into a concrete show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' cuts CITY to CIT; 'entering' places it in REAL. The City is London's financial district.
explanation.definitionFit: A recital is a musical or poetry performance by one or a few artists.

clue.text: Study having had face-lift?

parts.note: mug is slang for face
lifted things are up

explanation.surface: Asks whether studying is like having cosmetic surgery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'face-lift' reads as cosmetic surgery, but its two halves are the two pieces: face raised.
explanation.definitionFit: To mug up is British slang for studying hard and fast, often for an exam.

clue.text: US and Canada's row gets more odious

parts.note: NA stands for North America, with the possessive S
a tier is a row of seats

explanation.surface: A row between the US and Canada gets uglier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'row' looks like a quarrel but is a line of seats, TIER.
explanation.definitionFit: Nastier is the comparative of nasty, meaning more unpleasant or hateful.

clue.text: Getting claws out, non-starter, though in need of them?

indicators.note: non-starter means the first letter is dropped

parts.note: getting one's claws out is being catty or spiteful

explanation.surface: A catty person who still needs those claws for scratching.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Getting claws out' means bitchy, being spiteful; without its first letter it means wanting a scratch, which is what the claws are needed for.
explanation.definitionFit: An itchy person needs claws or nails for a good scratch.

clue.text: Where Napoleon Bonaparte delivered source of drug, having admitted the strain of office work

indicators.note: having admitted means the plant name takes the other letters inside

parts.note: the coca plant is the source of cocaine
RSI, repetitive strain injury, is the ailment of desk workers

explanation.surface: Napoleon delivering drugs while suffering from typing strain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'delivered' means born, not handed over. RSI is repetitive strain injury.
explanation.definitionFit: Napoleon was born in Ajaccio on the Mediterranean island ruled by France.

clue.text: Setter may be hard at the end of the rainbow

indicators.note: at the end of puts the letter for hard after the rainbow

parts.note: Iris is the Greek goddess of the rainbow, and iris can mean a rainbow
H stands for hard on pencils

explanation.surface: A crossword setter might be hard to find at the end of a rainbow.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Setter' seems to be the compiler but is the dog: the Irish setter.
explanation.definitionFit: The Irish setter is a red-coated breed of gun dog.

clue.text: Graphical illustration of characters in Chapter 1

indicators.note: characters in means the letters of the next words are reused in a new order

parts.note: 1 is I in Roman numerals

explanation.surface: A graphic shown among the characters in the opening chapter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'characters' looks like fictional people but means letters: CHAPTER with I (1) rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: A pie chart is a circular diagram divided into slices to show proportions.

clue.text: Dickensian pervert

definitions.meaning: Oliver, the orphan of Dickens's novel, bears this surname
to pervert something is to distort its meaning

explanation.definitionFit: Oliver of Dickens's novel has this surname, and the verb means to distort or corrupt.

clue.text: US Civil War general's last words were foolishly apathetic and idle … then shot instantly — thud!

definitions.text: US Civil War general's last words

indicators.note: foolishly means the letters of the following words are arranged wrongly, so rearranged

explanation.surface: A general's dying words were apathetic and idle, then he was shot dead with a thud.
explanation.walkthrough: General John Sedgwick, mocking Confederate sharpshooters at Spotsylvania in 1864, was shot mid-sentence; 'and' is a link joining the fodder, and the cut-off last word reflects the shot.
explanation.definitionFit: Union general John Sedgwick famously said these words just before a sniper killed him.
